planting.note: Direct sow on bare, firmed soil in fall; winter cold and moisture break seed dormancy, and plants emerge as basal rosettes that bolt and bloom the following spring.

directions: Direct sow in fall onto firmed, lean soil in full sun and let winter weather naturally break seed dormancy; plains flax is a wiry, slender-stemmed native of the calcareous clay and caliche prairies of central and south Texas, including Blackland Prairie remnants, where it is easily overlooked among taller grasses until its flush of bloom. From spring through early summer, each thread-like stem opens a succession of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers with a reddish-orange eye, each lasting only a single morning before dropping its petals. It self-sows readily in open, undisturbed clay soil and functions as a short-lived perennial or biennial, returning year after year once a colony is established. Give it lean, well-drained to average soil and avoid heavy mulch or rich fertilization, both of which encourage floppy growth at the expense of flowering.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
Shinners & Mahler's Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas

planting.note: Direct sow in fall where the plant is to remain permanently; the deep taproot resists transplanting, and seedlings are often slow and erratic to establish, typically not flowering until their second year.

directions: Direct sow in fall in lean to average, well-drained clay or rocky soil, siting the plant where it can stay permanently since its long taproot makes transplanting impractical. Texas nerveray is a Texas and southern Oklahoma near-endemic of Blackland Prairie clay openings, Grand Prairie limestone flats, and the edges of Cross Timbers post oak woods, square-stemmed and coarse-leaved with large, bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads from April through June whose ray florets are conspicuously marked with raised, vein-like ribs — the source of both its scientific and common names. It tolerates light shade at a woodland edge as well as open prairie sun, and once established is drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free. The persistent basal foliage and sturdy stems make it a good textural anchor in a native prairie or savanna-edge planting, where its bloom overlaps with the first flush of summer composites.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
Shinners & Mahler's Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, disturbed ground; seedlings form a flat basal rosette that overwinters and bolts to flower the following spring.

directions: Direct sow in fall on bare or lightly disturbed clay or loam soil in full sun, where the resulting rosette will overwinter close to the ground before bolting in spring. Cutleaf evening primrose is a low, sprawling native of Blackland Prairie clay openings, overgrazed pasture, and roadside disturbance across much of Texas, with deeply cut, irregularly lobed leaves and pale yellow flowers that open in late afternoon and fade to a soft pinkish orange as they age. It thrives in exactly the compacted, lean, disturbed-clay conditions that challenge more delicate prairie forbs, making it a useful early-successional component of a naturalistic meadow restoration. Plants are short-lived — typically annual to biennial — but reseed readily to maintain a colony once a patch of open ground is available each fall.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare soil; seed germinates with cool-season rains and overwinters as a small rosette before flowering in early spring.

directions: Direct sow in fall onto bare clay or loam soil in full sun to light shade, matching the open Blackland Prairie flats and post oak savanna margins where this low, scrambling annual naturally occurs. Short, bristly, scale-like hairs cover the sprawling stems, and in early spring they are lined with small, pale lavender-blue, funnel-shaped flowers marked with a ring of purple spots near the throat — a distinctive feature that gives the plant its common name. It completes its life cycle quickly in cool weather, setting seed and dying back before summer heat arrives, so it pairs well with later-blooming perennials that fill the same ground afterward. Once established in a planting it self-sows reliably each fall, needing no irrigation beyond natural winter and spring rainfall.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
Shinners & Mahler's Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas
